An initial assessment of the drivers and enablers of the current political system and lessons learned from previous reform attempts. It will include analysis into future jurisdictions where IF may pose a threat to UK and developing countries’ interests: Specialist action-oriented research and analysis into IF systems and vulnerabilities related to specific geographies and themes. This will analyse a broad range of sources and data sets, and draw on expertise and information in think tanks, academia, and NGOs: Flexible advisory support to develop and strengthen technically sound and politically feasible IF responses and interventions to IF and sources of IF, drawing on deployable experts with deep sectoral expertise: Monitoring, evaluation, and lesson learning on ‘what works’ to enhance resilience to IF across the international system: and a hub for knowledge, evidence, learning, and expert partnerships on IF.

titles: Global Dashboard of Illicit Finance Vulnerabilities (ICE ODA Project)
descriptions: This project, led by Tax Justice Network with input from the University of Sussex, has three interlinked components. The first component will produce an update of bilateral and jurisdiction-level Illicit Financial Flows vulnerability assessments, based on secrecy and regulatory data and aggregate trade and investment flows. The second component will see the construction and analysis of granular datasets of investment stock values and network architectures in / by key countries and actors and concern. The final component will see the integration of FDI and sanctions datasets from component 2, with updated TJN IFF vulnerability assessment in component 1, to support fine-grained, targeted assessment of risks associated with IFFs from particular countries of interest. Illicit financial flows are when money or capital is illegally earned, utilised, or transferred between countries. Illicit financial flows can involve an array of actors at different levels – across both developing and wealthier countries. Developing countries rich in natural resources, as well as those with high volumes of trade with advanced economies, show particularly high levels of illicit outflows. This project is seeking to map those illicit financial flows, across multiple ODA jurisdictions, and to estimate and measure the scale and risks of illicit financial flows using three main indicators of IFF risks: vulnerability, exposure, and intensity.

These workshops represents a pivotal step towards realizing the vision of a national open science policy and a national scientific publishing platform in Sierra Leone. It builds on the foundation laid by the LIBSENSE/SLREN Open Science Conference and the Sierra Leonean Writers Series, aiming to empower local researchers and scholars. Through this initiative, we envision a future where Sierra Leonean scientific knowledge is easily accessible and recognized globally, contributing significantly to the international scientific discourse.

The pilot is expected to start with a scoping phase in March 2024 that includes an expert mission from India to South Africa to set out potential approaches to initiate and implement the pilot in the remainder of the 2024/25 financial year. The pilot will serve as the implementation and learning phase to test joint knowledge sharing and innovation transfer interventions and provide recommendations for future collaborations in other sectors and geographies. The Expert Mission to SA in February/March will enable the joint development of the programme of work for the Pilot project.

Deliberations at the conference will address the significant education sector challenges faced in Kano State. The key outcome of the conference would be the development of sustainable solutions that will promote access to quality education for all children in the state, particularly considering recent socioeconomic and security challenges in the state. This conference is a move towards accelerating progress towards achieving Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG4), as adopted by the United Nations in 2015. To support the Government of Bangladesh (GoB) to deliver an effective, inclusive and environmentally sustainable response and recovery from the COVID economic crisis. The ultimate beneficiaries are poor people and disadvantaged groups affected by COVID’s economic impacts, such as the loss of jobs, businesses, and livelihoods. To achieve this, the programme will influence, inform and support GoB to respond more effectively to their needs by improving the quality and impact of its economic policy in selected areas, such as green growth, job creation and domestic resource mobilisation. This will contribute to Global Goals 1 (No Poverty), 8 (Decent Work and Growth), 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), 13 (Climate Action) and 17 (Partnerships to finance sustainable development). The programme will generate data, analysis and research to help create demand for and inform policy change; support local think tanks to advise and influence GoB policies; and provide technical assistance.
